title: The register that rated everything medium
scenario:
You are the risk manager at a pet insurance company with 900 staff. Four AI uses are live or planned. A project manager filled in the first AI risk register using the course's three tiers: low, medium and high.

The COO asks you to review it before the board meeting. The exhibit shows the draft register.
exhibit:
AI risk register: DRAFT (made-up example data)

#  Use                         Output goes to   Can act?              Tier    Controls planned
A  Meeting-notes summary       staff            no                    low     author reads it
B  Website FAQ assistant       public           no                    medium  none yet
C  Claims helper               claims system    yes: marks claims     medium  weekly spot check
                                                up to EUR 300 as paid
D  Policy-renewal email draft  staff, then      no                    low     agent edits, sends
                               customer

Planned change for use A (next month):
  summaries will be emailed straight to vet clinics
  after each partner meeting, with no staff step.

questions.prompt: Which use is in the wrong tier today?

options.text: Use A, because meeting notes can include sensitive internal topics.
options.explanation: Today a member of staff reads every summary first, and it can't act. That fits low. (Next month is another question.)

options.text: Use C, which marks claims as paid, a money-risk action, so it is high tier.
options.explanation: Right. The lesson's second question is "Can it act?" Use C changes a payment record, so it belongs in the high tier.

options.text: Use D, because every email that reaches a customer must be high tier.
options.explanation: An agent edits and sends each draft, and the AI can't act. A reviewed draft is not an action with money risk.

options.text: Use B, because a public assistant without actions should be high tier.
options.explanation: Use B only writes text and can't act. Text that reaches the public is the medium tier; it needs controls, not a higher tier.

questions.prompt: Use B has no controls yet. Which set fits OpenAI's and Anthropic's guidance best?

options.text: Let it answer any question freely, and fix wrong answers when customers complain about them.
options.explanation: Both guides push controls before launch: OpenAI recommends red-teaming, and Anthropic suggests screening input first.

options.text: Ask a person to approve every answer before the website shows it to the visitor who asked.
options.explanation: That control fits high-tier actions. For a live FAQ, it is very slow, and the guides offer lighter controls that fit this tier.

options.text: Add a line to the prompt: "Never say anything wrong about our policies or our prices."
options.explanation: An instruction can't supply missing facts. Anthropic's hallucination guide says its techniques reduce errors but don't remove them.

options.text: Answer from approved FAQ pages, screen input, limit its length, and red-team before launch.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's guide suggests validated materials, limited input and red-teaming. Anthropic's jailbreak guide suggests a small model that screens input.

questions.prompt: Use C moves to the high tier. Which control plan fits the guidance?

options.text: The helper proposes each payment and a claims handler approves it first, with no other write access.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's guidance pauses sensitive actions for human review. Anthropic's jailbreak guide applies least privilege: only the access it needs.

options.text: Keep the weekly spot check, but raise the sample from 10 claims to 50 claims each week.
options.explanation: A spot check finds errors after the money is paid. The high tier needs a check before the action.

options.text: Give it full access to the claims system, so it can also fix its own mistakes quickly.
options.explanation: More access means more damage if something goes wrong. Anthropic's guide recommends the narrowest access possible.

options.text: Lower the limit from EUR 300 to EUR 100, and keep everything else about the setup the same.
options.explanation: A lower limit reduces the size of each error, but the helper still pays without a person's approval.

questions.prompt: Next month, use A will email summaries straight to vet clinics. What should you do?

options.text: Nothing. It was rated low once, and the tier stays with the use no matter what changes.
options.explanation: The lesson says to re-check the tier when the audience changes. Here it changes from staff to outside clinics.

options.text: Move it to the high tier, because any email sent to outside people is automatically high risk.
options.explanation: It still only writes text and can't act. Reaching outside readers moves it to medium, not high.

options.text: Re-tier it to medium, since outsiders now read it first, and add controls before the change.
options.explanation: Right. The audience changed from staff to clinics. That is a trigger to re-tier and add controls before the change goes live.

options.text: Keep it low, but add a disclaimer line saying the summary was written by an AI system.
options.explanation: A disclaimer doesn't check facts. Outside readers now see the output first, so the tier must change.
